newsitem.title: FRANCE: Domestic factors protect French bond market.
newsitem.headline: Domestic factors protect French bond market.

text.p: While fears of U.S. monetary tightening rattle European bond investors, the French market looks the best protected thanks to the small percentage of domestic debt in outside hands, economists say.

While nobody expects France to escape unscathed from a big shakeout in the U.S. debt market, "we expect it to fall relatively less than other European markets -- essentially because foreign ownership of domestic debt is so low," said Marie Owens-Thomsen of Banque International du Placement.
Most recent official figures for December 1996 showed just 12 percent of outstanding French government notes and bonds was in foreign hands. That compared with nearly 40 percent in 1994.
"That, in itself, insulates France from any big speculative flows in capital," Owens-Thomsen said. In Germany, by contrast, non-resident investors hold 38 percent of the market.
"German debt is much more exposed and is, in that sense, one of the riskiest European markets," said another analyst.
Also supporting the French market is a massive reallocation of savings under way since last year as investors shift out of money market funds in response to falling interest rates.
This reallocation is believed to have injected 16 billion to 20 billion francs into the bond market in the first quarter and around 7.5 billion francs into equities.
"Our forecast for the year as a whole is that 80 to 100 billion francs will move into the bond market," Owens-Thomsen said. "That is about a fifth of the issuance programme of the French treasury."

During 1996, about 450 to 500 billion francs are believed to have flowed from money market funds and Livret A savings plans into longer term savings such as life insurance contracts which are mostly invested in bonds.

To this bond friendly environment, analysts say, can be added low domestic interest rates, slow growth, high unemployment and weak inflation. Inflation rose just 0.1 percent in March from February and was up 1.1 percent on the year.
These events are reflected in the yields of French 10-year bonds or Obligations Assimilables du Tresor (OATs) over their German counterparts.

In 1990, French 10-year OATs yielded two percentage points more than Bunds but the gap has closed and French yields are lower. Ten-year Bunds were yielding 13 basis more than OATs on Monday and analysts said that gap could widen to 18.
"These foreign holdings in the market are so small that France, by default, is outperforming Germany in a falling market," said Phyllis Reed of BZW.

Still, analysts say, the French bond market could be close to reaching its peak, especially with European monetary union, which should bring yields in France and Germany to parity when it goes into effect on January 1, 1999.
"If we really believe in monetary union, the investor will look at Bunds as cheap OATs," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais, adding the French market could be vulnerable to "some correction."
At the same time, though, analysts say restrictions barring life insurers from putting more than 20 percent of their holdings in foreign assets rules out a big exodus.
Also, economists say, the traditionally cautious pattern of French investment favouring domestic bonds means there will be no swift move into equities and foreign markets.

Once French interest rates start rising, the flow out of money market funds that have supported the domestic bond market will start to dry up "as the French like to keep their money in money," said one economist.
